title: Japan's Largest Power Company JERA Teams Up with Five Tech Giants to Co-Build AI Data Centers Beside Power Plants

content_html:
As global tech giants rack their brains over the training and inference of large models with hundreds of billions of parameters, an unavoidable law of physics is becoming a sword of Damocles hanging over their heads: the explosive growth of computing power will ultimately be paid for by electricity.

Recently, according to media reports, JERA, Japan's largest power producer, has formally entered talks with top global tech giants such as Anthropic, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google, planning to build large data centers directly near power plants in the Tokyo area. This major move not only opens a new chapter in Asia's AI infrastructure layout, but also confirms a new global trend of deep integration between "computing power + electricity."

 ⚡ Key Move: Break with Tradition and Build Data Centers at the "Energy Source"

Traditional data center site selection usually prioritizes network hubs or land costs, with electricity connected only as a supporting resource. But JERA's proposal to "build data centers near power plants" is a disruptive "build where the power is" strategy.

This integrated "generation, grid, load, and storage" model directly addresses two major pain points in today's AI industry:

1. Solving energy consumption and transmission losses: AI servers consume several times more power than traditional servers. Building data centers directly next to power plants can minimize long-distance transmission losses and ensure huge computing power clusters receive the most stable and efficient energy supply.

2. Direct green power supply and ESG compliance: As global tech giants commit to carbon neutrality, directly connecting to clean energy from power plants (such as LNG combined-cycle power generation or future planned green power) can provide AI companies with a highly attractive "zero-carbon computing power" solution, making it easier to clear increasingly strict environmental compliance thresholds.

 🤝 Industry Insight: From "Power Seller" to "AI Infrastructure Partner"

JERA's simultaneous talks with five top tech giants send a strong signal: energy companies are redefining their role in the AI industry chain.

In the past, power companies were merely behind-the-scenes infrastructure suppliers; now, facing exponential growth in electricity demand driven by AI, energy giants are taking the initiative and trying to become "co-builders" or even "ecosystem leaders" of AI infrastructure. This follows the same logic as Microsoft's recent restart of the Three Mile Island nuclear plant and Amazon's massive investment in a nuclear fusion startup—whoever controls stable, cheap, and sustainable energy holds the "physical layer" voice in the AI era.

 🌍 Strategic Significance: Japan's Positioning in Asia's AI Computing Power Landscape

Choosing the Tokyo area as a potential location is also strategically meaningful. As Japan's economic and technology center, the Tokyo area has a dense pool of tech talent, a well-developed network backbone, and huge enterprise-level demand for AI applications. If JERA can successfully implement the "electricity + computing power" model here, it will not only provide strong underlying support for the growth of Japan's domestic AI industry, but also potentially attract multinational tech companies to establish important Asia-Pacific computing power nodes here.

Of course, challenges remain. Japan's unique geological conditions place extremely high demands on data centers' earthquake resistance and disaster prevention, while large-scale concentrated construction will also need to face approval and environmental reviews from local communities.

But regardless, JERA's contact with the five tech giants has already pointed to a clear direction of evolution for global AI infrastructure: future tech competition has long moved beyond a simple contest of code and chips. On the runaway path of silicon-based intelligence, whoever is first to close the loop of "energy–computing power–application" will truly have the last laugh.
